title: Recover Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting a copy and comparing positions versus a single inorder pass detecting drops directly.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: The values of exactly two nodes of a binary search tree have been swapped by mistake, corrupting its BST property. Recover the tree WITHOUT changing its structure, by fixing it in place.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a BST with exactly two nodes' values swapped"],["Output","The same tree structure, with those two values swapped back correctly"],["Key Insight","A valid BST's inorder traversal is strictly increasing; a swap creates one or two \"drops\" that pinpoint exactly which two nodes were swapped"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"A BST's inorder traversal is normally sorted, but two values were swapped\"","Perform a single inorder traversal, tracking the previously visited node, and detect wherever the sequence unexpectedly \"drops\" (decreases) instead of strictly increasing"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

In a valid BST, an inorder traversal visits values in strictly increasing order. Swapping two nodes' values corrupts this in a very specific, recognizable way: if the swapped nodes are ADJACENT in the inorder sequence, exactly ONE "drop" appears; if they are NOT adjacent, exactly TWO separate "drops" appear. In both cases, the FIRST node of the first drop and the SECOND node of the last drop are exactly the two nodes that need their values swapped back.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Two Misfiled Documents in an Otherwise Perfectly Sorted Filing Cabinet
blocks.text: Picture a filing cabinet where documents are supposed to be in strictly increasing order, but two documents got misfiled (swapped). Scanning through once and noting wherever the order unexpectedly breaks pinpoints exactly where the problem is, whether the two misfiled documents are next to each other or far apart.

blocks.caption: A valid BST's inorder traversal is strictly increasing; drops in the sequence pinpoint the swapped nodes

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [1, 3, null, null, 2]
Recovered preorder: 3 1 null 2 null null null. The inorder sequence before recovery is 3, 1 (a single drop at adjacent nodes 3 and 1), so those two values are swapped back.
Example: tree = [3, 1, 4, null, null, 2]
Recovered preorder: 2 1 null null 4 3 null null null. The inorder sequence before recovery is 1, 3, 2, 4 (a single drop between non-adjacent-in-value 3 and 2), so those two values are swapped back.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A correct BST's inorder sequence is strictly increasing; a swap of two node VALUES creates a violation of this, detectable by comparing each visited node against the PREVIOUSLY visited one.

Observation 2: Whenever the previous node's value is GREATER than the current node's value (a "drop"), something is wrong at this point in the sequence.

Observation 3: If the two swapped nodes are adjacent in the inorder sequence, exactly ONE drop occurs, and both the "first" and "second" node of the swap are identified directly from that ONE drop (the previous node and the current node at that point).

Observation 4: If the two swapped nodes are NOT adjacent, exactly TWO separate drops occur; the correct nodes to swap back are the FIRST node of the FIRST drop and the SECOND node of the SECOND (later) drop, since those are the two nodes truly out of place, while what appears "between" them in the sequence is otherwise perfectly fine.
This leads to a single inorder traversal, tracking the previous node, recording the first and second node of the first drop found, and updating only the "second" node again if a LATER drop is found.
6. Brute Force Solution
Collect the full inorder sequence of node values into a list, sort a copy of that list, and compare position by position against the original to find exactly which two positions differ.
Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting a copy and comparing directly finds the two mismatched positions clearly.
This needs an extra O(n) sorted copy and a second full comparison pass, when detecting "drops" directly during a single inorder traversal finds the same two nodes without ever sorting anything.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the node list and the sorted copy.
Limitation: detecting "drops" directly during a single inorder pass finds the two swapped nodes without any sorting or extra full-size copies.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain three variables: first, second (both initially null, tracking the two nodes to eventually swap), and prev (the previously visited node during the inorder traversal, initially null). Perform an inorder traversal: whenever prev is not null AND prev.val is greater than the current node's value (a drop), if first is still null, set first to prev (this is the FIRST drop's earlier node); ALWAYS set second to the current node (so that if a SECOND, later drop occurs, second gets correctly updated to that later drop's second node, which is what actually needs fixing). After the traversal completes, swap first.val and second.val directly.
Perform a single inorder traversal, tracking the previous node, recording the two nodes whose values need to be swapped based on where drops occur.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for tree = [3, 1, 4, null, null, 2] (inorder before fixing: 1, 3, 2, 4)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison","Drop?","Action"],"rows":[["1 then 3","no (increasing)","continue"],["3 then 2","YES, 3 > 2","first = node(3), second = node(2)"],["2 then 4","no (increasing)","continue"],["Final swap","","swap values of node(3) and node(2): 3 and 2 exchange, restoring 1,2,3,4"]]}

codes.python:
def recover_tree(root):
    first = second = prev = None
    def inorder(node):
        nonlocal first, second, prev
        if node is None:
            return
        inorder(node.left)
        if prev and prev.val > node.val:                     # a 'drop' detected
            if first is None:
                first = prev                                       # earlier node of the FIRST drop
            second = node                                           # always updated, catches a LATER drop too
        prev = node
        inorder(node.right)
    inorder(root)
    first.val, second.val = second.val, first.val             # swap the values back

blocks.text: Why This Works

Detecting "drops" directly during the inorder traversal correctly identifies the exact two nodes whose values are out of place: the first drop's earlier node is always the true "first" swapped node, and always updating "second" to the current node at every drop found ensures that if a SECOND, later drop occurs (the non-adjacent swap case), second correctly ends up as the true "second" swapped node rather than an intermediate node that just happened to be involved in the first drop.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single traversal.
Space: O(h) recursion depth, O(1) extra beyond that.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Recover Binary Search Tree rewards recognizing that a valid BST's inorder traversal is strictly increasing, and that violations of this (drops) directly pinpoint the exact nodes to fix, in a single pass.
Common Mistakes

items: Only setting "second" on the FIRST drop found, and never updating it again on a later drop, which incorrectly handles the non-adjacent swap case.
Forgetting to actually SWAP THE VALUES (not the node references or structure), since the tree's shape must remain unchanged, only the values need correcting.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["The two swapped nodes are adjacent in the inorder sequence","Exactly one drop occurs; both first and second are correctly identified from that single drop."],["The two swapped nodes are far apart in the inorder sequence","Exactly two drops occur; first comes from the earlier drop, second is correctly updated by the later drop."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "always update second on every drop found, not just the first" heads off the most common bug in the non-adjacent swap case.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "exactly two nodes of a BST were swapped, fix it in place", think: a single inorder traversal detecting "drops" against the previously visited node.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve this using only O(1) extra space (beyond recursion), using Morris inorder traversal instead of regular recursion?

items: Validate Binary Search Tree, which relies on the same core fact that a valid BST's inorder traversal is strictly increasing.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The sort-and-compare approach costs O(n log n); the single-pass drop-detection approach costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a single inorder traversal detecting "drops" (violations of the strictly increasing property) against the previously visited node.
Core Idea: the first drop's earlier node is always the first swapped node; always updating "second" on every drop found correctly handles both adjacent and non-adjacent swaps.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(h) recursion depth for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: always updating "second" (not just on the first drop) correctly handles the non-adjacent swap case.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, moderately tricky medium to hard tree problem.
One line memory trick: track drops in inorder; first drop gives "first", every drop updates "second".
